Flight plan

Houston, we have a dust problem.

We're two students who like maths. We picked a problem that hasn't mattered much for planning yet: once people live on the Moon, a landing next to their base must not go wrong. So we rebuilt the 1969 dust storm with millions of virtual grains to work out how far is far enough.

Chapter 1 · April 1967

Meet Surveyor 3

Before anyone set foot on the Moon, someone had to check that the ground wouldn't swallow the lander. That job went to a robot. It is still standing up there.

Its mission

Your job: follow Surveyor 3 from launch to its last signal. Want the soil measurements? Open nerd mode.

Mission timeline

17 Apr 1967

Launch from Cape Kennedy, Florida.

20 Apr 1967

Shiny rocks confuse its radar and the engine keeps firing. Two bounces, up to 10 m high. Not in the manual.

Late Apr 1967

Digs four trenches with its scoop and sends 6,326 pictures to Earth.

4 May 1967

Two days into the two-week lunar night, Surveyor sends its last signal and never wakes up.

Nov 1969

Visitors arrive. That's chapter 2.

Nerd mode: what Surveyor 3 measured

The surface sampler (the scoop on its folding arm) could dig, scrape and press on the soil. From how hard its motor had to push, engineers estimated how strong the ground is: loose and fluffy on top, much firmer a few centimetres down. That told NASA an Apollo lander would not sink.

Surveyor 3's own landing was an accident with a bonus: highly reflective rocks confused its descent radar, so the engine did not cut off at 4.3 m. It bounced to 10 m, then to 3 m, and the footpad prints showed how the soil compresses.

In numbers: the scoop reached 1.5 m from the lander and dug up to 18 cm deep. Surveyor 3 dug four trenches and made four bearing tests and thirteen impact tests. Result: the soil behaves like wet sand and holds about 0.7 kg/cm² (98 kPa), enough for an Apollo lunar module. Launch mass 998 kg. Its TV camera had 25 mm and 100 mm lenses under a movable mirror and needed about 20 seconds per 200-line picture.

Sources: NASA Science, "Surveyor 3" mission page; NASA NSSDC photo catalogue (AS12-H-48-7100, AS12-H-48-7121); NASA SP-284 "Analysis of Surveyor 3 material and photographs returned by Apollo 12" (1972).

End of chapter 1
Chapter 2 · November 1969

Apollo 12 drops by

Mission goal: land a crewed spacecraft right next to another one. Target: Surveyor 3. Precision landing: GO. Sandblasting the target: not in the flight plan.

Station 1 of 3

The landing

Your job: read how Apollo 12 came down right next to Surveyor 3, in four steps.

1
14 Nov 1969

Launch into a storm

Apollo 12 launches into rain clouds. Lightning hits the rocket twice in the first minute, and the crew flies on.

2
19 Nov 1969, 06:54 UT

A pinpoint landing

Pete Conrad steers the lander Intrepid down just 155 m from Surveyor 3. It proves astronauts can land exactly where they plan.

3
The last metres

A sandblaster

The engine blasts the ground. Dust shoots out sideways, only a few degrees above the surface, and the finest grains fly faster than a rifle bullet. Some of it heads straight for Surveyor.

4
20 Nov 1969

Pieces of Surveyor go home

On their second moonwalk Conrad and Alan Bean walk over, cut off the camera, the scoop and some tubing, and bring about 10 kg of Surveyor parts back to Earth.

Station 3 of 3

The evidence

Your job: look at what the dust did to Surveyor's metal and paint. These pits are the one real measurement behind our model: they set the scale of every number on the map.

What scientists found back on Earth
103 pits per cm²

On metal from the side that faced the lander, scientists counted about 103 tiny pits in every square centimetre, each about as wide as a hair (around 80 µm). The square on the left is 1 cm × 1 cm, drawn with that many pits.

The side facing away was much cleaner: Surveyor 3 had been sandblasted by Apollo 12's engine.

How far away was Surveyor 3? Reports say 155 m (NASA SP-284) or "about 180 m". The LRO-based coordinates in NASA's NSSDCA catalogue (lander 3.0128° S, 23.4219° W; Surveyor 3 3.0162° S, 336.582° E) give 157 m, so our model uses 155 m.

More from the catalogue: Intrepid's descent stage is 4.2 m across, its footpads span 9.4 m, and its engine could throttle up to about 45 kN. After the crew left, the empty ascent stage was crashed into the Moon on purpose, and the seismometer they had just set up recorded the first artificial moonquake.

Photogrammetry of the Apollo landing films puts the dust ejection angle at 1.4° to 8.1° depending on the landing, most of them between 1.4° and 3.3° (Immer, Lane, Metzger, Clements). Pit shapes on Surveyor suggest impact speeds of a few hundred to about 2000 m/s (Brownlee et al. 1972).

End of chapter 2
Chapter 3 · the model

Rebuilding the dust storm

Flying a lander to the Moon to test this is slightly over our budget. So we throw 10 million virtual dust grains instead and count where they land. It works like finding out how often a dart hits the bullseye: throw thousands of darts and count. The method is named Monte Carlo, after the famous casino, because it runs on chance. So are we.

Station 1 of 3

How the model works

Your job: click the four tabs, or just watch. Each one shows one step, from the engine blast to the pit in the metal.

Nerd mode: the maths
Station 2 of 3

Throw the dice yourself

Your job: pick a target distance and press Throw 1,000 a few times. Watch the estimate settle. That is Monte Carlo: random grains, counted hits.

Grains thrown0
Hits on target0
Hits per million grains–

The band shrinks like 1/√N: four times more grains, half the uncertainty. Our real model throws 10 million grains for each of 36 model versions and 6 lander sizes.

Nerd mode: what this mini model does

Grain sizes follow a log-normal distribution (1–500 µm). Speed comes from Lane & Metzger's fit u ≈ 2054 / √D[µm] m/s, with a random spread for different launch points. Launch angle: one of the six Apollo film angles ± 0.5°. Flight: ballistic in lunar gravity with Moon curvature. A hit means the grain passes the target distance less than 1.5 m above the ground, so it would strike hardware 1.5 m tall.

estimate p = hits / N, uncertainty = 1.96 · √(p(1 − p) / N)

It is a simplified teaching version: the real model also computes how much dust each part of the ground releases at each moment of the descent.

Station 3 of 3

Why is the range so big?

Researchers still disagree on how exhaust lifts dust and at what angle it flies. Instead of picking one answer, we run 36 versions built from the main competing choices (3 erosion laws × 2 speed models × 6 angles) and show the spread. Your job: switch them off and watch how much the estimate moves.

Erosion law
Grain speed model
Ejection angle (from the Apollo films)

Outside the modelled range. We haven't tested the model above twice the Apollo LM's thrust, and landers this big may dig a crater under the engine, which the model leaves out.

Each line is one model version, for hardware 1.5 m tall. Coloured lines pass the pit test, grey ones don't.

Chapter 4 · the future

How far is far enough?

Moon bases are coming, and so are landers bigger than Apollo's, landing again and again. Flight control needs an answer: where can they touch down without sandblasting everything around them?

There's no single answer. We estimate where the sandblasting falls below a level we picked, using Surveyor 3 as the only real measurement. Treat it as a rule of thumb, not a safety rule.

Station 1 of 3

Sandblast map

Pick a site and a lander, then tap the map where it should touch down. The rings work like the circles around a campfire, where the smoke gets thinner the farther away you sit. Inside the innermost ring, hardware would be sandblasted at least as hard as Surveyor 3 was in 1969. The next rings mark 10 times and 100 times less.

The rings are estimates from our model, not safety limits. Press ▶ Replay Apollo 12 (1969) to see the Apollo 12 landing on the same map.

Planning tools

Your job: pick what to protect and which lander is coming. The advisor tells you how far away to land. Below: how much a landing pad or a berm helps.

Planning tool

Landing advisor

± 100 m
Protection

Pads, berms and craters

A landing pad is a hard, flat surface, like a helipad, so the engine finds no loose dust right under it to blow away. A berm is a ring wall of piled-up soil around the landing spot (50 m out in our model) that catches dust flying low, the way a fence stops a ball rolling along the ground.

Station 3 of 3

Why it matters

Your job: see what is still standing on the Moon, then read what we learned and where our model stops.

Heritage

Left behind on the Moon

Surveyor 3 is not alone. Hardware from every Apollo landing is still up there, and future landings near these sites need the same care.

NASA's own guideline. In 2011 NASA asked anyone landing near these sites to touch down at least 2 km from Apollo and Surveyor landers, or farther if their 3σ landing uncertainty is larger, and to approach along a tangent to that circle rather than straight at it. The reasoning: the lunar horizon is roughly 1.8 km away, so from 2 km the main sheet of fast dust flies over the hardware. These are recommendations, not legal requirements.

Facts from NASA Science mission pages, NASA's NSSDCA catalogue and NASA's 2011 recommendations for lunar heritage sites.

Wrap-up

What we learned

Final report

Engineers have studied this since Apollo 12 brought pieces of Surveyor 3 home. What's still open is how it scales: the next landers are far heavier than Apollo's, and the only hard data we have are the parts brought back in 1969.
